source: Forces in Circular Motion
A real force such as tension, friction or gravity supplies the net inward force mv²/r.
Students add an outward "centrifugal force" to the free-body diagram, or think a released ball flies straight outward.

If an object has Centripetal Acceleration, the second law says a net force must point toward the center too. That force isn't a new kind of force. Some real push or pull, one you can name, does the job.

For motion in a circle, the net inward force is $\role[net inward force]{force}{\Sigma F_{in}} = \dfrac{\role{mass}{m}\role[speed]{velocity}{v}^2}{\role[radius]{position}{r}}$. Tension, friction, gravity or a normal force supplies it. Nothing pushes outward.

Without an inward force, an object moves in a straight line (the first law). The inward force keeps bending its path. On a flat road, the only horizontal force on a car is static friction from the road, so friction must supply all of $mv^2/r$; that sets a top speed, $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$. For the Moon, Earth's gravity does the job; for a ball on a string, the tension does.
When the string is cut, the inward force disappears and the ball leaves along the tangent, not straight outward.
On a flat curve, static friction points toward the center and supplies mv²/r.
Worked examples
A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ puck on frictionless ice circles a post at $4\ \text{m/s}$ on a $1.2\ \text{m}$ string. Find the tension.
Tension in a string
about $6.67\ \text{N}$
The string is the only horizontal force: $T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{(0.5)(16)}{1.2}$.
$T \approx 6.67\ \text{N}$.
How fast can a car take a flat curve of radius $40\ \text{m}$ if $\mu_s = 0.7$?
Top speed on a flat curve
about $16.6\ \text{m/s}$
At the limit, $\mu_s mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The mass cancels.
$$v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r} = \sqrt{0.7 \times 9.8 \times 40} \approx 16.6\ \text{m/s}.$$

Adding an outward "centrifugal force" to the free-body diagram, or thinking a released ball flies straight outward. In a turning car you feel pushed outward because your body tends to keep going straight while the car turns under you. Check: every arrow on the diagram must be exerted by a real object, and a released object moves along the tangent.
